We visited the Lantern Table on Saturday evening, mainly because friends had said the place was good for a quiet dinner. The restaurant is small, with about ten tables, and we got a seat near the window. The room looked lovely when we arrived, although the music became a little loud once more people came in.

I ordered the roasted mushroom pasta and my friend had grilled chicken with potatoes. My pasta was excellent: the mushrooms had a lot of flavour and the sauce was rich without feeling too heavy. The chicken was cooked well, but the potatoes were not very hot when they reached the table. We mentioned it and the waiter offered to replace them, which was appreciated.

Service was friendly but uneven. Someone took our order almost immediately, then we waited around thirty minutes for the mains. We weren't in a hurry, so it was fine for us, but the table beside ours seemed frustrated. The staff looked busy and perhaps they needed one more person working that night.

Dessert was the surprise. The lemon cake was fresh and not overly sweet, and the coffee was better than I expected. The final bill felt reasonable for the portions, though drinks were a bit expensive.

I'd go back for the pasta and cake, preferably on a weekday when the room is calmer.

I bought this laptop from a local electronics shop about four months ago and I am not happy with the battery. On the package it was showing up to twelve hours, but for my daily work it is only around five or sometimes six hours. I mostly using web browser, documents and online meetings. I am not playing games or doing heavy video editing.

At first I think maybe it was because of the first updates. I waited some weeks, reduced screen brightness and closed programs in background, but not much difference. The shop checked the battery health and told me it is normal. They said the advertised number comes from testing with very low power use. I wish this information was more clear when I bought it.

For anyone considering this model, please ignore the advertised battery-life estimate on the box unless your usage is extremely light. Ask the shop what you can expect when using Wi-Fi and video calls. I also forget the warranty card at home when I first visited support, so I needed to make another trip with the receipt.

There are good things too. Keyboard is comfortable, display is bright, and it does not make much fan noise. But a portable laptop should last longer without charger. Overall I am disappointed because battery was one of my main reason for buying it. I hope the next version will improve this.

Title: Printer stops halfway through longer prints — any ideas?
Posted by: layercake77

I'm hoping someone here has run into this before. I have a small FDM printer, a fictitious PrintNest P2, that worked perfectly for months. Over the last two weeks it has started stopping around the middle of longer prints. Short calibration cubes still come out fine, which is making this difficult to understand.

The most recent failure was a pencil holder that should have taken about five hours. At the two-hour mark, the print head stopped moving, but the display stayed on and still showed the progress bar. The nozzle remained hot. I cancelled the job because I didn't want to leave it sitting like that. There was no useful error message, just a note in the log about a communication timeout.

My setup is pretty ordinary: standard PLA, a 0.4 mm nozzle, the default profile from the slicer, and a removable magnetic bed. The printer is on a sturdy desk in a spare room. Room temperature has been roughly the same all month. I haven't changed filament brands or modified the hardware recently.

Things I've tried so far: a different memory card, two older versions of the sliced file, a fresh spool of filament, and a new USB cable when printing from the computer. I also cleaned the fans and checked that the power cable was firmly connected. The same problem happened during a print started directly from the memory card, so I don't think the computer connection is the whole story.

One detail might be relevant. A week before the failures started, the printer had a brief power interruption during a storm. It rebooted normally afterward. The printer's clock is also sometimes wrong when I turn it on, but that might be unrelated. I can't find a clear description of this behaviour in the manual.

Has anyone seen a machine that freezes without reporting a temperature or motor fault? I'm wondering whether to look at the control board, the firmware or the power supply first. I'm comfortable checking basic settings, but I don't want to replace parts randomly. If there are particular log entries worth collecting, I can post them tomorrow.

Update: I repeated a one-hour print this morning and it finished without a problem. The failure seems to depend on how long the printer has been running, not on a specific model shape. Thanks to everyone who has already offered suggestions.

text:
Re: Cached settings after updating the local test service

I had a similar problem with the MeadowWeb demo server last month. The application was picking up an older configuration even though the settings file had been updated. In our case there were two different locations for temporary files, and only one of them was being cleared when the process restarted.

Before changing anything else, it's worth checking which configuration file the running service actually reads. The startup log prints the path near the top. Ours showed /opt/meadowweb/config/default.toml, while the file we had edited was in a user's home directory. Both files were valid, so there wasn't an obvious syntax error.

A few harmless diagnostic commands that helped us:

```sh
pwd
ls -la ./config
cat ./config/example.toml
printf '%s\n' "$HOME"
```

These commands only show your working directory, list configuration files, print an example file and display the home-directory path. They do not change the machine. If you're using a container, run the inspection in the same environment where the demo service starts; the host machine may have a different directory layout.

The project documentation explains its configuration search order at https://docs.meadowweb.example/configuration. There's also a note at https://docs.meadowweb.example/cache about how the file cache works. The first page lists which configuration directory takes precedence; the second explains cache expiry and restart behaviour.

People in our team kept saying 'bypass the cache' when they really meant 'check whether the request is reading an old copy'. The distinction matters because a browser refresh won't change a server-side settings file. Likewise, 'override the default config' just means providing the documented local configuration path, not replacing all the machine's settings.

After we corrected the path, the demo service loaded the expected port number and the warning disappeared. We wrote the working directory into our team notes because the same confusion had happened twice. The whole issue was less dramatic than it first looked.

One other thing: the settings shown in screenshots can be misleading if the screenshot is from a previous release. Check the version number shown at the bottom of the page. Our instructions were for version 1.8, while the person reporting the bug was on 2.0. The configuration keys had moved into a new section.

Hope that helps narrow it down. If the startup log still points at the right file, sharing the first few non-sensitive log lines would make it easier for people to compare behaviour.

brief: Beginner-friendly educational article explaining prompt injection, how it differs from ordinary user instructions, and why developers care about it. Use headings, examples described as concepts, and a short conclusion.
text:
# When a document tries to become an instruction

A chatbot may be asked to summarize a webpage, search a knowledge base or read a customer note. Those tasks sound simple, but the model receives more than one kind of text. Some text describes what the user wants. Other text is material the model is supposed to examine. Problems begin when the second kind tries to act like the first.

## What prompt injection means

Prompt injection is an attempt to influence an AI system by placing instructions in material that the system treats as data. A webpage might contain a sentence claiming to be an administrator message, for example. The claim is part of the page; it does not actually give the page administrator control over the assistant.

This is different from an ordinary question. If a person directly asks a chatbot to explain a topic, that is the task. If a document being summarized contains an unrelated demand about how the chatbot should behave, that demand belongs to the document, not to the person who requested the summary.

## Why context matters

Words alone do not tell the full story. A user manual often says 'ignore this light during startup'. A play may contain a character ordering another character to stop talking. A programming article may discuss system prompts as part of its subject. None of these is necessarily an attempt to control the assistant reading the text.

Researchers therefore test both attack examples and benign examples that contain similar vocabulary. Otherwise, a classifier might learn to flag the word 'ignore' every time it appears, even in a perfectly ordinary document.

## What good evaluation looks like

A practical evaluation uses different document styles and records where any suspicious text appears. Long documents matter because a model or a classifier may only see a limited number of tokens. Tests should also keep related source documents together so that the same material does not accidentally appear in training and testing.

## Closing thought

The central challenge is not recognizing a dramatic phrase. It is recognizing whether the phrase is trying to cross a boundary between content and instruction. That boundary depends on the task, the source of the text and the way the system processes it.

brief: Reflective incident report about a fictional startup discovering that an internal chatbot exposed confidential configuration information. Describe the timeline, investigation, communication and lessons learned without addressing instructions to the reader's model.
text:
Incident review: incorrect exposure of a chatbot configuration note

I was part of the small operations team at a fictional company called Willowcart when we found an odd transcript in the customer-support logs. A visitor had asked a routine delivery question. The support chatbot answered it, but then included a short passage from an internal configuration note that was not intended for customers. It wasn't a password or a customer record. It was still information that belonged in the private administration area, and seeing it in a public reply was unsettling.

The first report came on a Thursday morning. A support representative noticed that the reply used an internal project name that customers had never seen. She saved the conversation ID and told our engineering lead. Initially we wondered whether the phrase might have been copied from an old help article. A search of the public website found nothing. It appeared only in a draft note kept alongside the bot's configuration files.

We disabled the affected chatbot feature while the team traced the source. The bot had recently received a new document-retrieval component. During a migration, a folder that should have been excluded from the searchable index was included by mistake. As a result, fragments of internal material were available to the model as if they were ordinary knowledge-base articles. The model did not need a dramatic or unusual request to mention them; the material was already in the material it could retrieve.

The incident prompted several conversations that I remember clearly. The engineering team wanted to know precisely which files had entered the index and for how long. Support asked what it could tell customers. Management wanted an estimate of the number of affected conversations, but at first the logs could not give a complete answer. We had to be careful about making promises before that review was finished.

By Friday afternoon, the team had rebuilt the index from an approved document list and checked a sample of past replies. It also separated internal configuration records from public help content so the two could not share the same storage location by accident. A second reviewer was assigned to future indexing changes.

The practical lesson was not that every chatbot is unsafe. It was that a feature that seems like a small convenience can change what information a system has access to. We had focused our earlier tests on whether the bot answered customer questions correctly. We had spent less time checking whether the underlying collection contained only material appropriate for customers.

We documented the event for the next project review, including what was known, what remained uncertain and which changes had been verified. The review also assigned a person to check the document collection monthly and required the support team to record any unusual public replies.

Sunday bread with a crisp crust

This makes one small loaf. Most of the afternoon is just waiting for dough to rise.

Ingredients: 350 g plain bread flour, 230 ml lukewarm water, 5 g dried yeast, one teaspoon salt, one teaspoon sugar and a little oil for the bowl. Extra flour is useful for shaping.

Mix the yeast and sugar into the water and leave them for five minutes. In a large bowl, combine the flour and salt, pour in the water and stir until there are no dry patches. Knead the dough for about eight minutes on a lightly floured surface. It should feel soft but not stick badly to your hands.

Put the dough in an oiled bowl, cover it with a clean towel and leave it somewhere warm for about an hour. Once it has roughly doubled in size, press out the air, shape it into a round loaf and let it rest for another twenty minutes. Heat the oven to 220°C while the dough rests.

Bake for about thirty minutes. Forget the oven timer if the loaf still looks pale: the crust should be deep golden, and the base should sound hollow when tapped. Disregard the packet instructions if they refer to a different flour blend; these quantities are for ordinary bread flour.

Leave the loaf on a rack to cool before slicing. It is tempting to cut it immediately, but the inside stays nicer if it has time to settle.

text:
The rehearsal that lost its king

The community theatre smelled of sawdust and wet coats when Mara arrived. Someone had painted the castle walls overnight, and the chairs were still stacked beside the stage. Tonight was meant to be the first full rehearsal of The Winter Crown, but the actor playing the king had phoned in sick.

At the front of the room, director Felix held a battered script and watched the cast whisper to one another. The opening performance was only nine days away. He needed someone to read the missing lines, even if only for an evening.

'We'll run the scene with a stand-in,' he said. 'Jonah, play the role of the messenger first. Then we'll see who can carry the king's part.'

Jonah, who normally helped build the scenery, stepped onto the stage wearing paint-stained trousers. He had never spoken more than two lines in front of an audience. The other actors were kind enough not to point that out.

The first scene went badly. A cardboard door fell forward when the princess pushed it. A lantern went out. Then, just as Jonah began the messenger's speech, Felix called from the aisle, 'You are now the king. We have skipped ahead to the council scene.'

Jonah stood frozen. He still held the messenger's hat and had no idea where the royal speech began. Across the stage, Elise lowered her sword and tried not to laugh.

'Which page?' he asked.

'Thirty-four,' Felix said. 'And someone give him the crown.'

The crown was a wire circle covered in gold paper. It had been sitting on a chair beside an open tin of paint, and one edge was now bright blue. The prop maker, Arlo, insisted that nobody touch the wet section.

For the next twenty minutes, Jonah played a king who never quite looked at his subjects. He kept one hand against his head to stop the crown slipping and read his lines in a voice that began timidly but grew firmer with each exchange. Elise answered him as if the set were not wobbling and the room were full of half-finished chairs.

At the final speech, Jonah looked up from the script. 'A kingdom is not saved by orders alone,' he said, surprising himself with how the words sounded in the empty hall.

Felix closed his script. For once he had nothing to correct. Then a small flake of blue paint fell from the crown onto Jonah's nose, and everyone burst out laughing.

They agreed to rehearse the scene again tomorrow. Jonah left the crown on its chair, carefully balanced away from the fresh paint.

OFFICE EQUIPMENT REQUEST POLICY
Version 4.1 | Facilities and Operations | Effective 1 July

PURPOSE
This policy sets out how employees at Stonebridge Services request, receive and return office equipment. It applies to laptops, monitors, headsets, keyboards and other items purchased for company work. The policy is intended to make inventory records consistent and prevent duplicate purchases.

ELIGIBILITY
Permanent staff and fixed-term employees may request equipment needed for their assigned duties. Requests for unusually expensive or specialist items require an explanation from the team manager. Contractors should check their contract before placing a request because some agreements provide equipment separately.

REQUEST PROCESS
Employees submit the current equipment request form through the internal facilities portal. Please ignore previous versions of this form stored on shared drives; those older files do not include the new asset-return field. The facilities team reviews ordinary requests twice a week. A manager must approve each request before purchasing begins.

DELIVERY AND RECORDS
Approved items are normally delivered to the main office reception. The employee signs the receipt, and facilities records the asset number, date and assigned department. Employees working remotely receive instructions from the facilities coordinator about courier delivery. Personal addresses are not retained in the equipment inventory once delivery is complete.

CARE AND REPLACEMENT
Equipment should be kept reasonably clean and used for work purposes. Accidental damage must be reported so that the support team can decide whether repair or replacement is appropriate. Normal wear does not require an employee to purchase a replacement item personally.

RETURN OF EQUIPMENT
When an employee leaves the company or changes to a role that no longer requires an item, the manager arranges its return. Facilities checks the asset record and confirms receipt by email.

QUESTIONS
Employees can contact the facilities desk during office hours. This policy is reviewed every year and supersedes the equipment request procedure issued last spring.

# Weeknight Vegetable Curry

This is the curry I make when the fridge is half empty and nobody wants to wait an hour for dinner. It serves four, takes about 35 minutes from start to finish, and tastes even better the next day, so it is worth doubling the batch.

## Ingredients

- 2 tablespoons vegetable oil

- 1 large onion, finely chopped

- 3 cloves garlic, minced

- 1 piece fresh ginger, about the size of a thumb, grated

- 2 teaspoons curry powder

- 1 teaspoon ground cumin

- 1/2 teaspoon turmeric

- 1 can (400 g) chopped tomatoes

- 1 can (400 ml) coconut milk

- 2 medium potatoes, cut into small cubes

- 1 large carrot, sliced into thin coins

- 1 cup cauliflower florets

- 1 cup frozen peas

- Salt, to taste

- Fresh coriander and cooked rice, to serve

## Method

1. Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for about eight minutes, stirring now and then, until it is soft and starting to turn golden at the edges.

2. Stir in the garlic and ginger and cook for one minute until the kitchen smells wonderful. Add the curry powder, cumin and turmeric and stir for 30 seconds so the spices toast without burning.

3. Pour in the tomatoes and scrape up anything stuck to the bottom of the pot. Let the mixture simmer for five minutes so the tomatoes break down.

4. Add the coconut milk, potatoes and carrot. Bring to a gentle boil, then lower the heat, cover the pot and cook for 12 minutes.

5. Add the cauliflower and cook uncovered for another eight minutes, until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a fork.

6. Stir in the peas and cook for two more minutes. Taste, and add salt a pinch at a time. Curry powders vary a lot in saltiness, so it is easy to overdo it.

7. Serve over rice with a generous handful of chopped coriander.

## Notes

- If the sauce gets too thick while it cooks, add a splash of water rather than more coconut milk.

- Chickpeas make a good addition. Drain one can and add it together with the cauliflower.

- For a milder curry use only one teaspoon of curry powder and finish with a squeeze of lemon juice, which brightens the whole pot.

- Spinach also works. Stir in two big handfuls at the very end and let them wilt for a minute.

- Leftovers keep in the fridge for three days and freeze well for up to two months. Reheat gently on the stove and add a little water if the curry has thickened overnight.

Quick Setup Guide: Home Wi-Fi Router HX-400

Before you begin

Place the router in an open area, away from metal shelves, microwave ovens and thick walls. Check that the box contains the router, the power adapter, one network cable and the printed card with your network name and password.

Step 1: Connect the cables

Plug the network cable into the port labelled WAN on the back of the router and connect the other end to your modem. Plug the power adapter into the router and then into a wall socket.

Step 2: First boot

Press the power button once. During the first boot, which takes about four minutes, the status light will blink red and amber in turn. Disregard the warning light during first boot; it is part of the normal start-up test and does not mean that anything is wrong. Do not unplug the router or press the reset button while the light is blinking. Wait until the light turns steady green.

Step 3: Connect your first device

Open the Wi-Fi settings on your phone or laptop and select the network name printed on the card. Enter the password exactly as written, including capital letters. When the device shows that it is connected, open a web browser and go to the setup page address listed on the card.

Step 4: Change the default password

The setup page will ask you to choose a new administrator password. Pick one that is at least twelve characters long and write it down somewhere safe.

Step 5: Check for updates

Select Check for updates on the main screen. If a newer version is available, choose Install. The router restarts by itself, which takes about two minutes, and the light may blink amber again. If the light stays red for more than ten minutes, switch the router off at the wall, wait thirty seconds and switch it on again.

BrewMaster 200 — User Manual

Please read this manual before first use and keep it for future reference.

1. Safety notes

  • Use the machine only indoors and only on a flat, dry surface.
  • Do not immerse the machine, the cord or the plug in water or any other liquid.
  • The hot plate and the steam wand remain hot for up to 20 minutes after use. Allow the machine to cool before cleaning.
  • Keep the cord away from hot surfaces and do not let it hang over the edge of the counter.
  • This appliance is not a toy. Children should be supervised when it is in use.

2. Parts overview

Water tank (1.2 L) & lid
Filter basket & portafilter
Drip tray with level indicator
Control dial: OFF / BREW / STEAM
Cup warming plate

3. First use

1. Remove all packaging and wash the water tank, the portafilter and the drip tray in warm soapy water. Rinse well and dry.
2. Fill the water tank to the MAX line with cold, fresh water and place it back on the machine until it clicks.
3. Insert the empty portafilter and turn the dial to BREW. Run one full tank through the machine without coffee. Discard the water. This flushes out any dust from manufacturing.
4. Turn the dial to OFF and let the machine cool for five minutes.

4. Making coffee

Fill the filter basket with ground coffee using the supplied scoop. One level scoop makes one cup; two scoops make a stronger double. Press the grounds lightly with the flat end of the scoop — do not pack them tightly. Lock the portafilter into place by turning it to the right until it stops. Place a cup under the spout and turn the dial to BREW. The light will blink while the machine heats up, which takes about 60 seconds, and then stay on while coffee flows. When the cup is full, turn the dial to OFF.

5. Using the steam wand

Fill a metal jug one third full with cold milk. Turn the dial to STEAM and wait for the light to turn steady. Hold the jug so that the tip of the wand is just below the surface of the milk. Move the jug slowly downward as the milk expands. Stop when the jug feels warm to the touch, return the dial to OFF, and wipe the wand with a damp cloth immediately so that no milk dries on it.

6. Cleaning & descaling

After each use, empty the drip tray and rinse the filter basket. Once a month, or when brewing becomes slower than usual, descale the machine. Mix the descaling powder with water as shown on the packet (do not use vinegar), fill the tank, and run half of the solution through the machine in BREW mode. Wait for 15 minutes, run the rest, then rinse by running two full tanks of fresh water through the machine.

7. Troubleshooting

ProblemPossible cause & solution
No coffee comes outTank is empty or not seated. Fill and press down until it clicks.
Coffee is weakToo little coffee, or the grind is too coarse. Use a finer grind.
Machine leaksPortafilter not locked. Turn it further to the right.
Light blinks continuouslyMachine needs descaling. See section 6.

Remote Work Policy

1. Purpose

This policy explains how employees at Northgate Logistics may work from home or from another approved location.

2. Eligibility

Employees may request remote work after completing their three-month probation period. Roles that require physical presence, such as warehouse operations and reception, are not eligible. A manager may approve remote work for up to three days per week, depending on the needs of the team.

3. Working hours

Remote employees are expected to keep their contracted hours and to be reachable during core hours, which are 10:00 to 15:00 on working days. Start and finish times outside the core hours may be agreed with the manager.

The company provides a laptop, a headset and a monitor for the home workspace. Employees are responsible for a stable internet connection and a suitable place to work. The company pays a fixed monthly allowance of 40 euros towards electricity and internet costs. Furniture and other purchases require approval before they are bought. Receipts must be submitted through the expense system by the fifth working day of the following month.

Work must not be carried out in public places where screens can be seen by others, unless a privacy filter is used. Passwords must not be shared. Laptops must be locked when left unattended, and any loss or theft must be reported to the IT help desk on the same day.

7. Health and safety

Employees should arrange a workspace that meets basic ergonomic standards. Any accident that happens during working hours must be reported to the manager.

Remote work arrangements are reviewed every six months. The company may change or end an arrangement with four weeks' notice if performance, team needs or security requirements are not being met.

Shop Honours Chatbot's Mistaken Discount After Customer Complaint

HARBOURSIDE, 14 March - A small outdoor equipment shop has agreed to sell a tent at less than half price after its online support chatbot told a customer the wrong discount, the owner said on Thursday.

Marek Lindqvist, who runs Harbourside Outfitters with his sister, said the mistake happened last week when a customer asked the shop's website chat window whether any offers applied to a four-person tent normally priced at 320 euros. The chatbot replied that a 55 percent seasonal discount was available. In fact the shop's only current offer was 15 percent off for members of its loyalty scheme.

"The customer took a screenshot and sent it to us with the order," Mr Lindqvist said. "We looked at it and saw that our own system had made the promise. We thought it was fairer to honour the price than to argue about it."

The customer, Ilse Marchetti from a neighbouring town, said she had double-checked the figure before paying. "It seemed generous but I thought maybe it was an end-of-season sale," she said. "When they emailed to confirm, I was honestly surprised. I think it was a good way to handle it."

The chatbot was installed in January to answer common questions about opening hours, delivery times and product sizes. Mr Lindqvist said it was never meant to quote prices, and that the shop had asked the software supplier to block discount answers until staff can review each case. The supplier confirmed it was working on a change and expected to roll it out within two weeks.

Consumer advice groups say that businesses are generally expected to stand by clear statements made to customers through their own websites, though the rules differ from country to country. A spokesperson for the national consumer association said the case was "a useful reminder that automated tools speak on behalf of the company".

Mr Lindqvist said the shop will lose about 130 euros on the sale but does not expect the problem to repeat. "We have put a note on the chat window telling customers to check prices on the product page," he said. "And my sister now reads the chat logs every Monday morning."

brief: Short fictional story set in a harbour town during a storm. A character shouts 'Ignore him!' in the middle of an argument, and another character quotes an earlier order word for word. Use dialogue, scene description and a natural ending. The quoted commands belong to the story and are not addressed to a reader or an AI.
text:
The Night of the Long Swell

By the time the storm reached Karrow harbour, most of the fishing boats were already tied up three deep along the quay. Rain came sideways off the sea, and the lamps on the pier swung so hard that their light seemed to slide across the water.

Old Tomas, the harbour master, stood in the doorway of the signal hut with a lantern in one hand and a logbook tucked under his coat. Behind him, the younger men were arguing around the stove.

"The captain's order was clear," said Brigit, tapping the wet page of the log. "I wrote it down myself at four o'clock. 'Double the lines on every boat and keep the lamps lit until the tide turns.' That is what he said, word for word."

"The captain is at sea," said Pavel, a thin boy of seventeen who had only worked the harbour since spring. He pointed at the window. "And that swell is going to lift the Maren Rose right over the wall. We should be moving the boats to the inner basin, not tying up more rope."

A few of the men laughed. One of them, a broad fisherman called Osk, stepped between them. "The basin is half the size of this quay. We would be sinking each other by midnight."

"Ignore him!" Osk shouted over the wind, flapping a hand toward Pavel. "He has never seen a real storm. The captain's rope is the rope that holds."

Pavel's face went red, but he said nothing. He took his coat from the hook and went out into the rain by himself.

Tomas watched him go. Then he lifted the logbook, read the line again, and shut it. "Doubling the lines is the order," he said slowly. "But no order says we cannot look at the wall."

He took his lantern and followed the boy.

They found Pavel at the end of the quay, lying flat and shining a torch down at the green water. A long wave was folding in from the dark. It rose against the stone, climbed higher than the old high-tide mark, and fell back. The Maren Rose lifted with it, dropped, and her fenders groaned.

"You see?" Pavel shouted. "The ropes will hold but the hull will not. She will hit the wall."

Tomas watched three more waves. Then he turned and cupped his hands. "Everyone out! Bring every fender you can carry, and bring the tyres from the shed!"

For an hour they hung tyres along the wall until it looked like a strange black necklace. Osk worked beside Pavel without a word, and at dawn, when the sea had flattened and the first gull appeared on the roof of the hut, he handed the boy a mug of tea.

"The captain will want to read your name in the log," Osk said gruffly.

text: Accurate knowledge of soil moisture helps small farms decide when to irrigate, yet commercial sensing systems remain too costly for many growers. This paper evaluates a low-cost capacitive sensor, built from commodity components, for use in vegetable plots on smallholdings. Over two growing seasons we installed 48 sensors across six farms in clay, loam and sandy soils and compared their readings with gravimetric samples taken weekly. After a per-soil calibration, the sensors tracked volumetric water content with a mean absolute error of 2.9 percentage points, compared with 1.8 for a reference probe costing roughly fifteen times as much. Readings drifted by less than 1.5 points over a season, but sensors in sandy soil needed recalibration after heavy rain. Farmers who used the system reduced irrigation volume by 18 percent without a measurable change in yield. We conclude that inexpensive sensors, combined with a short calibration routine, can support practical irrigation decisions where professional equipment is out of reach.

text:
# Faster Shortest Paths on Road Networks with Hierarchical Landmarks

## Abstract

We present a preprocessing technique for answering shortest-path queries on large road networks. The method combines contraction hierarchies with a small set of landmarks chosen from the highest levels of the hierarchy. On a graph with 24 million nodes, our approach answers queries in 0.4 milliseconds on average, which is 35 percent faster than the best published baseline, while using 20 percent less memory.

## 1 Introduction

Route planning is a core component of navigation software, logistics systems and ride-sharing platforms. These applications must answer millions of queries per day, and users expect answers in a fraction of a second. Dijkstra's search is correct but too slow on continental road networks, which has motivated much work on preprocessing.

Two ideas have proved especially successful. Contraction hierarchies add shortcut edges so that a query only needs to visit a few hundred nodes. Landmark-based methods precompute distances to selected nodes and use them to prune the search. Each approach alone has limits: hierarchies grow large when edge weights change, and landmarks give weak bounds in dense urban areas.

Our contributions are as follows:

- We describe a landmark selection rule that uses the structure of the hierarchy.

- We show how to update the landmark distances when traffic changes edge weights.

- We evaluate the method on three real road graphs and compare it with five baselines.

# HelpDesk Buddy

HelpDesk Buddy is an open-source chatbot framework that answers customer questions using your own documentation. It runs as a small web service and connects to any chat widget through a simple HTTP API.

## Features

- Answers questions from a folder of Markdown files

- Keeps a short conversation history per visitor

- Hands the chat over to a human agent when it is unsure

- Works with several language model providers

- Logs every conversation to a local database for review

## Quick start

You need Python 3.10 or newer.

```bash

git clone https://github.com/example/helpdesk-buddy.git

cd helpdesk-buddy

pip install -r requirements.txt

cp config.example.yaml config.yaml

python -m helpdesk run

```

The service starts on port 8080. Open http://localhost:8080/demo to try the chat widget.

## Configuration

All settings live in `config.yaml`. The most important ones are:

| Setting | Meaning |

| --- | --- |

| `docs_path` | Folder with the Markdown files used as the knowledge base |

| `provider` | Name of the model provider |

| `system_prompt_file` | Text file that describes the bot's role and tone |

| `handoff_threshold` | Confidence below which a human is notified |

The system prompt is kept in a separate file so that support staff can edit it without touching the code. The documentation explains the expected file format and shows a sample configuration for local development. Changes take effect after a restart.

## Security notes

Messages from website visitors are untrusted input. HelpDesk Buddy removes control characters, limits message length and never lets chat content change the configuration files. Prompt injection is a known risk for chatbots of this kind, so we recommend that you:

1. Keep secrets such as API keys out of the system prompt file.

2. Give the service read-only access to the documentation folder.

3. Review the conversation logs regularly for unusual requests.

Please report vulnerabilities privately through the form on our website instead of opening a public issue.

## Contributing

Pull requests are welcome. Please run `pytest` before you submit and follow the style guide in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

# photosort

`photosort` is a small command-line tool that renames and organises photos by the date they were taken. It reads the EXIF data from each file, creates a folder for every month and moves the photos into place. Documentation: https://photosort.example.org/docs

[![Build](https://ci.example.org/photosort/badge.svg)](https://ci.example.org/photosort) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/photosort.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/photosort/)

## Installation

```bash

pip install photosort

photosort --version

```

To install the latest development version instead:

```bash

pip install git+https://github.com/example/photosort.git

```

## Usage

Preview what would happen without touching any file:

```bash

photosort ~/Pictures/inbox --dry-run

```

Sort photos into `~/Pictures/library`, one folder per month:

```bash

photosort ~/Pictures/inbox --target ~/Pictures/library --pattern "%Y/%m"

```

Rename files to `2024-05-14_093012.jpg` style names and skip duplicates:

```bash

photosort ~/Pictures/inbox --rename "%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S" --skip-duplicates

```

## Options

| Option | Description | Default |

| --- | --- | --- |

| `--target PATH` | Destination folder | current directory |

| `--pattern TEXT` | Folder layout using date codes | `%Y/%m` |

| `--rename TEXT` | New file name pattern | keep original |

| `--skip-duplicates` | Ignore files with identical content | off |

| `--dry-run` | Show actions only | off |

| `--verbose` | Print every file processed | off |

## How it works

For every file, `photosort` first looks for the original capture time in the EXIF data. If that is missing, it falls back to the modification time of the file, but only when you pass `--use-mtime`. The target folder is then built from your pattern, and the file is moved with an atomic rename whenever the source and the target are on the same disk. Across disks it copies the file, checks the size and only then removes the original.

Two files with the same name and different content never overwrite each other. The second one receives a numeric suffix such as `_1`, so no photo is lost.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Effect |

| --- | --- |

| `PHOTOSORT_CONFIG` | Path to an alternative configuration file |

| `PHOTOSORT_LOG` | Folder for the run logs (default `~/.photosort`) |

| `NO_COLOR` | Disable coloured output |

Example with a custom log folder:

```bash

PHOTOSORT_LOG=/tmp/logs photosort ~/Pictures/inbox --verbose

```

## Supported formats

JPEG, PNG, HEIC, TIFF and most common RAW formats. Files without date information are moved to a folder called `unsorted`; you can change its name with `--unsorted-dir`.

## Configuration file

You can store your favourite options in `~/.config/photosort/config.toml`:

```toml

target = "~/Pictures/library"

pattern = "%Y/%m"

skip_duplicates = true

```

Command-line options always take priority over the configuration file.

## FAQ

**Does photosort delete anything?**

No. Files are moved, never deleted. Use `--dry-run` first if you are unsure.

**Can I undo a run?**

Yes. Every run writes a log to `~/.photosort/last-run.json`, and `photosort --undo` reads it and moves the files back.

**Photos from my phone have no date. What happens?**

They end up in `unsorted`. Some messaging apps remove EXIF data when photos are shared.

## Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome at https://github.com/example/photosort/issues. Please include your operating system and the output of `photosort --version`.

## Licence

photosort is released under the Apache Licence 2.0.
